lesson: Two different totals can constrain the same unknown counts. Suppose every small packet holds 2 cards and every large packet holds 5. A fictional record lists 9 complete packets containing 30 cards altogether. Let s be the number of small packets and l the number of large packets. The packet equation is s + l = 9; the contents equation is 2s + 5l = 30. Label the variables so that packet counts are not confused with card counts.

The first equation gives s = 9 - l. Substitute that expression into the second: 2(9 - l) + 5l = 30. Expanding gives 18 - 2l + 5l = 30, so 3l = 12 and l = 4. Then s = 5. Check both original statements: 5 + 4 = 9 packets, and 2 x 5 + 5 x 4 = 30 cards.

A proposed answer must fit the context as well as the equations. Packet counts must be nonnegative whole numbers. If the record instead claimed 9 packets and 31 cards, the same method gives l = 13/3, which is not a whole number. Do not round that to a nearby count and call the record reconciled. Under these assumptions the pair of totals has no valid packet-count solution.

An inconsistency does not identify which record is wrong. There could be a transcription error, an incomplete packet, an unrecorded packet type or a mistaken contents rule. Preserve the original entries, note the failed check and seek additional evidence. Algebra tests the compatibility of an account; it does not authorize silently rewriting an observed total to make the model work.
practice: There are 10 complete packets of the same two types and 32 cards altogether. Write the equations and solve for each type.
Check the answer using both the packet total and the contents total.
A record claims 10 complete packets and 33 cards under these same rules. Explain why rounding an algebraic result would not resolve the discrepancy.
answers: s + l = 10 and 2s + 5l = 32. Substituting s = 10 - l gives 20 + 3l = 32, so l = 4 and s = 6.
The equations give l = 13/3, not an allowable whole packet count. Rounding would fail at least one original total. The records or model assumptions need investigation.
lessons.adaptation: Start with packet cards to check a candidate by counting. Learners can then connect the substitution step to replacing every small-packet count with the remaining number of packets.

lessons.title: Read rounded values as intervals with stated limits
lessons.audience: Beginning learners with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Find the interval represented by a rounded positive value and avoid confusing a rounding bound with a complete measurement-uncertainty assessment.
lessons.materials: Paper number lines and fictional lengths; use the rounding rule explicitly supplied in the lesson.
lesson: For this exercise, round positive lengths to the nearest whole centimetre and round an exact half upward. Under that rule a reported 18 cm represents an unrounded reading x with 17.5 <= x < 18.5 cm. The lower endpoint is included because 17.5 rounds to 18; the upper is excluded because 18.5 rounds to 19. Write the rule alongside the interval, since different tie conventions can change endpoint inclusion.

Consider two readings reported as 18 cm and 12 cm under that same rule. Their unrounded reading intervals are [17.5, 18.5) and [11.5, 12.5). Adding bounds gives a sum interval [29, 31) cm. The reported values sum to 30 cm, but the unrounded sum is not established as exactly 30. Square brackets mean an endpoint is included; parentheses mean it is excluded.

Now compare the information with a fictional paper requirement that the first unrounded reading be no greater than 18.2 cm. A report of 18 cm alone cannot establish that requirement: compatible readings lie on either side of 18.2. Record the outcome as unresolved with the available rounding information. More suitable evidence would be needed; inventing extra decimal places does not supply it.

These intervals describe only the rounding of a reading. They are not guaranteed bounds for the true object's length: calibration, alignment, environmental effects and other measurement issues are outside the model. Nor does an interval say every value within it is equally likely. Separate the mathematical consequence of an explicit rounding rule from any broader claim about measurement quality or compliance.
practice: Under the lesson's positive-value, half-up rule, what interval of unrounded readings is reported as 23 cm?
Add intervals for reported readings of 23 cm and 8 cm. What interval contains their unrounded sum under the model?
Does a rounded report of 23 cm establish that the unrounded reading is at most 23.1 cm? Explain, and name one uncertainty source outside this rounding model.
answers: The second interval is [7.5, 8.5), giving a sum in [30, 32) cm.
No. Compatible readings include values above and below 23.1 cm. Calibration error, alignment or environmental effects are examples of issues not covered by the rounding interval.
lessons.adaptation: Use open and filled endpoint marks as well as inequality words. Begin with the intervals of readings only, then explicitly discuss why they are not a complete description of the true length.

lessons.title: Combine group means using the number of observations
lessons.audience: Beginning learners with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Recover group totals from exact means and counts, then calculate a pooled mean without giving unequal groups equal weight by accident.
lessons.materials: Paper timing cards for fictional sorting trials, with one card per observation.
lesson: A mean is a total divided by a count. When combining non-overlapping groups of comparable observations, recover each group's total before pooling. If a group has n observations with an exact mean m, its total is n x m. The pooled mean is the sum of the group totals divided by the sum of their counts. This gives each observation equal weight rather than giving each group equal weight.

Use original trial times measured in minutes. Group A has two records, 4 and 6, so its total is 10 and mean is 5. Group B has six records, 8, 8, 9, 9, 10 and 10, so its total is 54 and mean is 9. Together there are eight records totaling 64 minutes, giving a mean of 8 minutes. Averaging the two group means gives 7, which answers a different question by weighting the groups equally.

If two groups have equal counts, the simple mean of their exact means does equal the pooled mean. Counts are the key, not whether the group labels look equally important. Also check units and eligibility: do both groups measure the same task definition, are all intended records included, and does any observation occur in both groups? Repeated records should not receive extra weight merely because they appear in two files.

Rounded means need care. Multiplying a rounded mean by a count gives an approximate total, not necessarily the original exact total. Preserve the underlying records or exact totals when possible, and label approximations. A pooled mean can also conceal group differences and variation within groups. Keep group counts and distributions available so a reader can see what the single number summarizes.
practice: Group C contains three observations with an exact mean of 4 minutes. Group D contains seven with an exact mean of 10 minutes. Calculate the pooled mean.
Two groups each contain five observations and have exact means of 6 and 10. Find the pooled mean and explain why averaging those means works here.
A report supplies only means rounded to whole minutes. Can multiplying them by group counts recover exact original totals? Explain.
answers: Totals are 3 x 4 = 12 and 7 x 10 = 70 minutes. Pooled mean = 82/10 = 8.2 minutes.
The totals are 30 and 50 across ten observations, so the pooled mean is 8. Equal group counts make the groups' weights equal.
Not in general. Rounding discarded information. The reconstructed totals and pooled mean may be approximate; raw records or exact totals would be needed for an exact reconstruction.
lessons.adaptation: Give each record one token and compare the number of tokens behind each mean. Learners can audit a pooled total by adding the original small data sets directly.

lessons.title: Choose the denominator in a two-way table
lessons.audience: Beginning learners with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Calculate overall, joint and conditional percentages from one table and explain why reversing a condition changes the denominator.
lessons.materials: Paper for a two-row envelope table using the fictional counts supplied below.
lesson: A two-way table classifies the same records by two attributes. In an original envelope inventory, color is blue or green and status is sealed or unsealed. Draw columns for sealed, unsealed and row total. The blue row is 12, 8, 20. The green row is 18, 42, 60. Column totals are 30 sealed and 50 unsealed, with 80 envelopes overall. The categories are exhaustive and mutually exclusive for this exercise.

Read the question before selecting the denominator. 'What percentage of all envelopes are sealed?' uses 30/80 = 37.5%. 'What percentage of blue envelopes are sealed?' restricts the group to the 20 blue envelopes, so it uses 12/20 = 60%. 'What percentage of sealed envelopes are blue?' restricts the group to the 30 sealed envelopes and uses 12/30 = 40%. The same cell count can support different fractions because the comparison groups differ.

A joint question asks for records satisfying both conditions out of the full collection. Blue and sealed accounts for 12/80 = 15% of all envelopes. If one envelope is selected uniformly at random from this defined collection, these proportions also describe the corresponding selection probabilities. The table by itself does not establish a probability for a different collection or a future process.

Check totals before interpreting. A missing status should not be silently entered as unsealed, and an envelope counted twice inflates both relevant totals. If categories or counts are incomplete, document how that affects the denominator. A difference between conditional percentages is an association in this inventory; it does not prove that an envelope's color caused its sealing status.
practice: What percentage of green envelopes are sealed? State the numerator and denominator.
What percentage of all envelopes are both blue and sealed? How does its denominator differ from 'sealed among blue'?
A learner claims '60% of blue envelopes are sealed, so 60% of sealed envelopes are blue.' Correct the second percentage and explain the change.
answers: 18/60 = 30%, using sealed green envelopes over all green envelopes.
12/80 = 15%. The joint percentage uses all 80 envelopes; 'sealed among blue' uses only the 20 blue envelopes.
12/30 = 40% of sealed envelopes are blue. Reversing the condition changes the reference group from all blue envelopes to all sealed envelopes.
lessons.adaptation: Circle the eligible row or column before counting its target cells. Use shape labels as well as color names; the task works with written category names alone.

lessons.title: Track successive percentage changes with factors
lessons.audience: Beginning learners with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Apply each percentage change to its current base and explain why equal percentage increases and decreases do not generally cancel.
lessons.materials: Paper arrows labeled starting amount, percentage factor and new amount; quantities are hypothetical.
lesson: An increase of p percent multiplies the current amount by 1 + p/100. A decrease of p percent multiplies it by 1 - p/100. State the base for each step. In an original quantity model, start at 200 units, increase by 10% to 220, then decrease that new amount by 10% to 198. The decrease removes 22 units, not the 20 units added in the first step.

Write the full chain before calculating: 200 x 1.10 x 0.90 = 198. The combined factor is 0.99, so the overall change is a 1% decrease from the original 200. Adding +10% and -10% would wrongly treat both changes as based on the original amount. It is the changing base that makes the two-step result different.

Repeated increases also compound. Two increases of 10% from 200 give 200 x 1.10 x 1.10 = 242, a 21% increase overall. To reverse a factor, use its reciprocal: after multiplying by 0.80, returning to the original amount requires multiplying by 1/0.80 = 1.25, an increase of 25%. Keep the intermediate amount visible to check what each percentage means.

These are deterministic paper rules, not forecasts. Real quantities may have varying rates, whole-item restrictions or rounding at each step. If rounding is part of the rule, record when it happens; do not silently round intermediate values and then report an exact result. For a decrease model, also check that the chosen percentage and domain make sense: subtracting more than the complete available amount would require a different interpretation.
practice: Start at 160 units, increase by 25%, then decrease the new amount by 25%. Find the final amount and overall percentage change.
Start at 100 units and apply two successive 20% increases. Find the final amount and overall percentage increase.
A quantity falls from 100 to 75. What percentage increase from 75 would restore it to 100?
answers: 160 x 1.25 = 200; 200 x 0.75 = 150. The net loss is 10/160 = 6.25% of the original amount.
100 x 1.20 x 1.20 = 144, an overall increase of 44%.
The required gain is 25 on a base of 75: 25/75 = 1/3, or 33 1/3%. The original decrease was 25%, but the restoring increase uses the smaller base.
lessons.adaptation: Use a base box for every step and write the percentage beside that box. Learners can first compute each change separately, then connect the sequence to multiplication factors.

lessons.title: Read a specification card with units, conditions and revision
lessons.audience: Beginning learners with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Extract a target, allowed interval, units, conditions and revision from a fictional specification without treating a label or one reading as complete evidence.
lessons.materials: Paper copies of the two fictional card specifications and observation record below; no manufactured device is being certified.
lesson: A specification can contain a nominal target, an allowed range and conditions for interpreting a result. These are different kinds of information. Use an original paper-card example: CARD-B, revision 2, states a nominal width of 82 mm and an allowed recorded-width interval of 81.5 to 82.5 mm inclusive. Its comparison rule uses a dry card lying flat and a record naming the measurement method. Here nominal means the named target, not a promise that every card measures exactly 82 mm.

Extract a compact checklist before comparing numbers: item identifier CARD-B; revision 2; quantity width; unit mm; inclusive limits 81.5 and 82.5; stated card condition; measurement-method record. A fictional record of 82.4 mm is numerically within those limits. If the method or condition is missing, report that omission separately instead of treating the number as complete evidence. The classroom rule is a reading exercise, not a general conformity-assessment procedure.

Revision matters. An earlier CARD-B revision 1 used a nominal width of 80 mm and limits of 79.5 to 80.5 mm. The task sheet explicitly calls for revision 2. Applying revision 1 would answer the wrong question even if the arithmetic were flawless. Record the required revision rather than selecting whichever limits happen to accept the reading or assuming an unlabeled sheet is current.

Units and evidence must also match. A width recorded as 8.24 cm equals 82.4 mm; a bare 8.24 without a unit cannot be compared reliably. Report the observation, its unit, relevant conditions and the rule used. Measurement uncertainty and actual object properties remain broader questions than a simple recorded-number comparison. Do not turn a fictional table check into a claim that real equipment or materials have been technically approved.
practice: For CARD-B revision 2, identify the nominal width, inclusive allowed interval and unit.
Convert a recorded 8.24 cm to millimetres and compare it numerically with revision 2. What missing record information would still need attention if only the number and unit were supplied?
Why would using revision 1 to reject an 82.4 mm record be the wrong comparison when the task explicitly requires revision 2?
answers: Nominal width is 82 mm; the inclusive interval is 81.5 to 82.5 mm.
8.24 cm = 82.4 mm, within the interval. The record still needs the stated condition and measurement method, along with clear item/revision identification, for the exercise's complete evidence check.
Revision 1 specifies different limits for an earlier definition. The required rule is revision 2, so a revision-1 verdict does not answer the assigned question.
lessons.adaptation: Mark each field with its name rather than relying on table position. A learner may dictate the extracted checklist and comparison while a partner records the exact units and revision.

lessons.title: Separate requirements, recommendations and options
lessons.audience: Beginning learners with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Read explicitly defined instruction levels and write an evidence checklist that does not confuse an optional feature with a requirement.
lessons.materials: Paper for an original classroom packet specification and three example packet records.
lesson: Technical documents sometimes define particular words to signal different instruction levels. Read the document's own convention before assigning a special meaning. RFC 2119 and its clarification RFC 8174 illustrate a scoped convention for technical specifications; their keyword meanings are not automatically rules for every ordinary use of 'must,' 'should' or 'may.' Our classroom specification below states its own small convention for the exercise.

In this original packet specification, MUST means required for this exercise, MUST NOT means prohibited, SHOULD means recommended with any departure explained, and MAY means optional. Its rules are: each packet MUST carry a unique ID; it MUST NOT contain a duplicate page; it SHOULD include a contents list; and it MAY have a colored cover. A plain cover therefore does not by itself show a failure to meet a required rule.

Inspect a fictional packet record: ID P-17 is present and unique within the supplied batch, pages have been checked with no duplicates, the contents list is omitted with the stated reason 'single-page packet,' and the cover is plain. The record supports the two mandatory checks, records an explained departure from the recommendation, and omits an optional feature. Evaluating whether the reason is convincing is a separate discussion; do not relabel the recommendation as a prohibition or call missing evidence a confirmed pass.

Make the checklist traceable. Copy or restate the rule accurately, name the evidence and record the result or what remains unknown. If the rule only says 'make the packet good,' ask for observable criteria before inventing a numerical threshold. A requirement's wording, scope and revision should stay attached to its check so that another reader can understand why the result was recorded.
practice: A packet meets the ID and duplicate-page rules but has a plain cover. Does the cover violate this specification? Explain.
A packet has a contents list and colored cover but no ID. Which instruction level is violated?
A record says 'duplicate-page check not done.' Should the mandatory no-duplicate rule be marked passed, failed or unverified from that record alone? Explain.
answers: No. A colored cover is optional under MAY. A plain cover is allowed by these stated rules.
It violates the MUST requirement for a unique ID. Recommended or optional features do not compensate for a missing mandatory item.
Unverified. The record supplies no completed check establishing whether duplicate pages are present; lack of evidence is not the same as a confirmed duplicate or a confirmed absence.
lessons.adaptation: Use separate cards for the four instruction levels and sort example rules by their stated meaning. Keep the fictional convention visible throughout the exercise.

lessons.title: Write a model-based plan with constraints and unresolved evidence
lessons.audience: Beginning learners with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Combine resource limits, time models and an evidence checklist in a short planning note that separates a feasible estimate from verified completion.
lessons.materials: Paper, the kit rules from lesson 140 and the fictional method/time rules supplied here; this is a planning exercise only.
lesson: Use this original planning brief: prepare at least 7 complete kits, including at least 3 type A, from 12 cards and 12 clips. Type A uses 2 cards and 1 clip; type B uses 1 card and 2 clips. The whole preparation must fit within a modeled 32-minute session. Write the requirements and units first. Reuse the inequalities from lesson 140, then add a + b >= 7 and a >= 3.

Test the candidate a = 3, b = 4. It produces 7 kits, uses 10 cards and 11 clips, and leaves 2 cards and 1 clip. Two fictional preparation methods include all setup and checking steps: method M takes 9 + 3n minutes and method N takes 18 + 2n, where n is the total kit count. At seven kits, M takes 30 minutes and N takes 32, so both fit the stated limit, with different modeled margins.

Revise one assumption at a time. If M's per-kit time is only known to lie from 3 to 3.5 minutes inclusive while its setup stays exactly 9, its seven-kit total lies from 30 to 33.5 minutes. The available bound no longer establishes completion within 32 minutes. N's stated 32-minute result is still a model assumption, not a timed observation. State what timing evidence and completed-kit checks would be needed before claiming the work actually met the brief.

Write a short note with the chosen counts, resource arithmetic, model and assumptions, comparison with the limit, unresolved evidence and next check. A possible beginning is: 'Three A and four B satisfy the stated stock and mix constraints. Method M predicts 30 minutes under the 3-minute rate assumption, but the revised range extends beyond the limit.' Keep this conditional conclusion visible. Correct arithmetic and a plausible plan do not establish that kits were produced, checked or delivered.
practice: Check the plan of four A and four B against stock and mix requirements. At eight kits, do either M or N fit the original 32-minute time limit?
For seven kits and M's revised rate interval of 3 to 3.5 minutes per kit, calculate the elapsed-time interval and explain the conclusion about the deadline.
Write a two- or three-sentence planning conclusion for three A and four B, including a resource result, a conditional timing result and one unresolved evidence need.
answers: Four A and four B use 12 cards and 12 clips and satisfy the minimum total and A-count requirements. M takes 9 + 24 = 33 minutes and N takes 18 + 16 = 34; neither fits 32 minutes under the original rules.
9 + 7 x 3 = 30 and 9 + 7 x 3.5 = 33.5, so the inclusive interval is [30, 33.5] minutes. It overlaps the deadline: the supplied range does not establish completion within 32 minutes.

Accept a conclusion that gives 7 kits using 10 cards and 11 clips, labels timing as conditional on the chosen model, acknowledges the revised timing range if using M, and requests relevant timing or kit-check evidence. Do not accept an unsupported claim that production or delivery has already succeeded.
lessons.adaptation: Allow an oral planning note supported by a labeled table. A facilitator can supply the formulas while the learner chooses the inputs, checks the constraints and explains the limits of the conclusion.

lessons.title: Choose a scientific word's meaning from its context
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Distinguish everyday and technical uses of a familiar word, and keep the technical definition tied to its stated object and conditions.
lessons.materials: Paper vocabulary cards for work, power, force, movement and time; a facilitator can preview or read all technical words aloud.
lesson: A familiar word can have a narrower meaning in a scientific passage. Read this original pair: 'Preparing the display took a lot of work.' 'A constant 5 N force moved the model block 2 m along the force, doing 10 J of work on the block.' The first uses work for effort or a task. The second uses a defined physics quantity. Choosing a meaning requires the sentence's context, not merely the word's spelling.

For the stated straight-line case with constant force along displacement, work by that force is force times displacement: 5 N x 2 m = 10 joules. If the block stays motionless, that force does zero mechanical work on the block in this model. This does not say a person holding something still uses no bodily energy. Identify whose force and which object's movement the technical statement concerns.

Power also has several everyday uses. In this exercise its technical meaning is the rate of energy transfer or work. Transferring 24 J in 6 seconds gives an average power of 4 watts, because one watt is one joule per second. Transferring the same 24 J in 3 seconds gives 8 W. The amount transferred is equal in the two cases, but the rates differ.

Build a context note with four fields: word, meaning here, sentence clue and an original example. For power, units such as J, s and W are useful clues, although units alone do not guarantee an explanation is correct. If a text shifts from an everyday sense to a technical one, make the change explicit. These vocabulary and arithmetic cards are paper models, not instructions for lifting or powered equipment.
practice: In 'The committee has the power to choose a date,' does power mean joules per second? Identify its sense here.
An ideal card states that a constant 7 N force moves an object 3 m along that force. Calculate work by the force, then state the result if the object has no displacement.
Two models each transfer 30 J, one in 5 seconds and the other in 10. Compare their average powers without claiming one transfers more total energy.
answers: No. It means authority or ability to make the decision in that sentence.
7 x 3 = 21 J. With zero displacement, that force does zero mechanical work on the object in the stated model.
30/5 = 6 W and 30/10 = 3 W. The first has twice the average power, but each transfers the same 30 J.
lessons.adaptation: Read the sentences aloud and allow oral context notes. Preview technical vocabulary before independent reading; the passage is not presented as a phonics-controlled text.

lessons.title: Follow a process passage that branches into several paths
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Translate a branching process description into labeled paths without turning possibilities into a compulsory sequence.
lessons.materials: Paper location cards and arrows; the entire original reading passage is supplied below.
lesson: Preview the words infiltration, runoff and evaporation. Infiltration is water entering the ground, runoff is water flowing over the land surface, and evaporation changes liquid water to water vapor. Read this original passage: 'Rain reaches a hillside. Some water enters the ground, while some travels over the surface toward a stream. Water in the ground may later reach a stream too. Some surface water evaporates. Water can also remain stored before it moves again.'

Turn the passage into branches from a rain-at-surface card. One path enters the ground; another follows the surface toward the stream; another represents evaporation to the atmosphere. Add a possible later connection from groundwater to the stream. Label arrows with processes and use a separate note for storage. Drawing every statement in one line would incorrectly suggest that all water first infiltrates, then runs off, then evaporates in that order.

Read the linking words closely. Some divides the account into portions without specifying their amounts. While can signal simultaneous or contrasting paths. May identifies a possibility rather than a guarantee. Later gives an order along a stated path but no duration. A passage can describe a mechanism without providing enough information to calculate how much water takes each route or how long its journey lasts.

Check a diagram by retelling each path in words and matching it to a sentence. The water cycle includes many connected stores and transfers beyond this short passage; it has no single required starting point. Our cards deliberately omit many details. Mark unsupported arrows as questions instead of quietly adding them as if the passage had supplied them.
practice: Name two different routes from the hillside surface to the stream that the passage allows.
Does 'some water enters the ground' mean exactly half of the rainfall infiltrates? Explain.
Rewrite 'All rainwater must flow over the surface before entering the ground' so it matches the passage's branching account.
answers: Water can flow over the surface toward the stream, or enter the ground and later reach a stream through the possible underground route described.
No. Some does not specify a fraction or volume; the passage supplies no amount for that branch.

One acceptable version: 'Some rainwater enters the ground, while some flows over the surface toward a stream.' Other versions must preserve the alternative paths and avoid an unsupported universal sequence.
lessons.adaptation: Use movable cards or dictate the paths. Discuss one branch at a time, and distinguish difficulty reading a technical word from difficulty understanding the process.

lessons.title: Read a scientific diagram's legend before its arrows
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Use an explicit legend to separate stores from transfers and avoid reading scale or timing information into an unlabeled schematic.
lessons.materials: Paper for three labeled boxes and arrows, or the complete verbal description below; no image is needed to answer the questions.
lesson: A diagram's symbols obtain their meaning from its labels and legend. For this original water-account schematic, draw boxes P, Q and R. The legend says boxes are stores and arrows show total water transferred during one specified day. An arrow P to Q is labeled 8 L; an arrow Q to R is labeled 5 L. Neither arrow's drawn length nor width encodes a quantity. The numbers, units and direction carry that information.

Read the schematic as sentences: 'During the day, 8 litres move from P into Q, and 5 litres move from Q into R.' If Q begins with 10 L and these are its only transfers, Q ends with 10 + 8 - 5 = 13 L. Its stored amount is different from either arrow's transfer amount. The diagram gives daily totals, not the exact timing or order of individual transfers within the day.

Move the boxes farther apart on paper without changing the labels. The represented account stays the same because the diagram is schematic, not a scale map. Make one arrow thicker; the quantity still comes from its 8 L or 5 L label under this legend. Another diagram could define thickness quantitatively, but that meaning must be stated rather than assumed from appearance.

Before interpreting an unfamiliar scientific diagram, identify what each symbol represents, what an arrow means, which units apply, and whether size or distance has a stated scale. Food-web arrows, force arrows and process arrows need not have the same meaning. If a necessary legend is missing, explain the ambiguity instead of guessing. A good reading names what the diagram communicates and what it leaves unspecified.
practice: Using the supplied schematic and Q's initial 10 L, calculate Q's final stored amount.
If the P-to-Q arrow is drawn twice as long, does that change its represented transfer from 8 L to 16 L under this legend?
Can the two daily arrow totals establish that all 8 L arrived before any of the 5 L left? Explain.
answers: 13 L, assuming the stated two transfers are the only ones affecting Q.
No. Arrow length has no quantitative meaning in this schematic. The label remains 8 L.
No. They specify total transfers over the day, not their timing or order within it.
lessons.adaptation: Use the verbal description alone, or add tactile boxes and arrows. Ask learners to explain the legend before performing the storage calculation.

lessons.title: Resolve pronouns and cause words in a science paragraph
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Identify what a pronoun refers to and revise an ambiguous process explanation without adding an unsupported cause.
lessons.materials: Paper copies of the original sentences below, with condensation previewed aloud as needed.
lesson: Scientific reading often depends on small linking words. Read this original account: 'Moist air surrounded a cool tile. Near the tile, the air cooled enough for some water vapor to condense on the surface. This change produced liquid droplets. The tile had been dry before the droplets appeared.' Here condensation names a change from water vapor to liquid; the water need not have come from inside the tile.

Ask what this change refers to. In this paragraph it points to water vapor condensing, not to the tile becoming a different substance. Replace the phrase with its referent to check meaning: 'Condensation of water vapor produced liquid droplets.' A pronoun or reference phrase should connect clearly enough that the reader can recover the intended object or process without inventing a new one.

Now inspect a weaker sentence: 'The tile touched the damp cloth after it cooled.' It might refer to the tile or to the cloth, so the sentence does not clearly identify what cooled. Two possible revisions are 'After the tile cooled, it touched the damp cloth' and 'The tile touched the damp cloth after the cloth cooled.' Choose only the revision supported by the intended record; editing should not silently decide an unknown fact.

Order and cause also differ. After tells us that one event followed another, while because asserts an explanatory connection. Replacing 'droplets appeared after the fan started' with 'droplets appeared because the fan started' strengthens the claim and requires supporting evidence. The original condensation account is a supplied scientific explanation, but a bare observation of a wet tile would not by itself exclude a spill, a splash or another source of water.
practice: In the original account, what does 'This change' refer to? Rewrite that sentence with the full process named.
The intended record says the cloth cooled first. Revise 'The tile touched the damp cloth after it cooled' to make that meaning clear.
Why is changing after to because more than a stylistic edit in a report of two events?
answers: It refers to water vapor condensing. One revision is 'Condensation of water vapor produced liquid droplets.'
'The tile touched the damp cloth after the cloth cooled.' Other clear versions preserving that order and referent are acceptable.
After states sequence; because claims a causal explanation. The stronger causal claim needs evidence beyond the order alone.
lessons.adaptation: Use different labels or underlining for each possible referent, rather than color alone. The facilitator can read the paragraph aloud and ask the learner to explain or dictate revisions.

lessons.title: Compare two process accounts using the same questions
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Compare evaporation and boiling by matched features, preserving both a shared change of state and the stated differences.
lessons.materials: Paper for a comparison grid and the two original short accounts below; no liquid is heated in this activity.
lesson: Read account A: 'Liquid water can become water vapor at its exposed surface without the whole liquid boiling. This surface process is evaporation. Its rate depends on conditions; a surface becoming dry does not imply that the water reached its boiling temperature.' Preview vapor as gaseous water. The account describes a process, not a complete experiment identifying every cause of a particular wet surface becoming dry.

Read account B: 'During boiling, vapor bubbles form within the liquid under suitable temperature and pressure conditions. The boiling temperature depends on pressure. Boiling and evaporation both involve liquid changing to gas, but the liquid-gas change can occur in different ways.' These sentences do not state that any visible bubble in water proves boiling; bubbles can have other origins, and the account specifically concerns vapor bubbles in boiling.

Compare the same features across both accounts: starting and ending states, where the described change occurs, and which conditions are mentioned. Both describe liquid becoming gas. A emphasizes the surface and the absence of a requirement that the whole liquid boil; B emphasizes vapor bubbles within the liquid and the role of pressure. A comparison that lists unrelated details in two separate columns may miss the actual relation between the processes.

Write a synthesis that keeps both shared and contrasting information: 'Both processes turn liquid into gas. Evaporation can occur at a surface below the boiling temperature, while boiling involves vapor bubbles forming within the liquid at conditions set in part by pressure.' Do not add a universal numerical boiling temperature without stating the substance and pressure. The goal is accurate comparative reading, not instructions for heating or testing containers.
practice: State one shared feature of evaporation and boiling supported by the accounts.
A summary says, 'Water must boil before any of it can become vapor.' Explain why that summary conflicts with account A.
Write a two-sentence comparison using the matched feature 'where the described change occurs,' and retain the condition about pressure from account B.
answers: Both involve liquid changing to gas; for water the gas is water vapor.
Account A says evaporation can occur at the exposed surface without the whole liquid boiling. The summary adds a requirement the account explicitly rejects.

Accept a comparison locating evaporation at the surface and vapor-bubble formation within boiling liquid, with a statement that boiling temperature depends on pressure. It should not give an unqualified temperature or claim that all bubbles mean boiling.
lessons.adaptation: Read each account aloud, preview evaporation and boiling, and fill one comparison row at a time. Learners can dictate the synthesis rather than independently decode every technical term.

lessons.title: Link a shadow claim to records and a ray explanation
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Separate a recorded pattern from a mechanism and write a claim whose scope matches a simplified shadow model.
lessons.materials: Paper ray lines and the supplied fictional shadow records; no lamp, laser or sun observation is required.
lesson: Use a supplied paper setup: a point-like light source is 60 cm from a screen. An opaque card 4 cm high is centered between them, parallel to the screen. Distance means source-to-card distance. Fictional records give 12 cm shadow height at 20 cm distance, 8 cm at 30 cm, and 6 cm at 40 cm. All other stated geometry stays the same. These numbers are invented illustrations of the ideal ray model, not actual measurements.

A narrow claim is 'In these three records, moving the card farther from the source and nearer the screen corresponds to a smaller shadow.' Support it with the distances and shadow heights, including units. The phrase 'the shadow gets smaller' alone leaves the reader unsure what moved, what stayed fixed and whether a size or a distance is being discussed.

Explain the pattern using straight ray paths from the point source past the card's upper and lower edges to the screen. When the card is nearer the source, those bounding rays spread farther apart by the time they reach the screen. The explanation connects geometry to the size pattern; it is different from merely repeating the three numbers. Real extended light sources and other arrangements can produce different edge details, so the point-source assumption matters.

Try a counter-question: if the screen distance also changed between records, could the same comparison isolate the effect of card position? No; that would introduce another change in the geometry. A useful explanation names the model and controlled features as well as the evidence. It does not claim that every shadow in every lighting arrangement obeys a slogan such as 'farther away always means smaller.'
practice: Which recorded card position gives the largest shadow, and what is that shadow's height? Specify what the position is measured from.
Write one evidence sentence comparing the 30 cm and 40 cm source-to-card records.
Why should an explanation mention that the light source and screen stay 60 cm apart?
answers: The card 20 cm from the source gives the largest listed shadow, 12 cm high.

One version: 'When source-to-card distance changes from 30 to 40 cm with the screen fixed, the listed shadow height decreases from 8 to 6 cm.' Equivalent wording must keep the quantities and units distinct.
Screen distance affects the projection geometry. Keeping it fixed supports this comparison; changing it would introduce another possible explanation for a size difference.
lessons.adaptation: Let a learner trace described rays on paper or use the numerical records alone. Accept an oral mechanism explanation with a facilitator supplying unfamiliar words.

lessons.title: Cross-check a scientific paragraph against its data table
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Audit each numerical statement against the correct row, unit and interval, and preserve missing data rather than filling it by assumption.
lessons.materials: Paper for the fictional temperature record and draft report supplied in the lesson; no temperature experiment is needed.
lesson: An original paper record lists one container's temperature in degrees Celsius: minute 0, 35; minute 5, 33; minute 10, 30; minute 15, not recorded. It contains three numerical observations and one missing entry. Read the table's quantity and unit before comparing it with a paragraph. The missing entry is not a zero-temperature observation and is not automatically a repeat of the preceding value.

Now audit this draft: 'The container cooled by 2 degrees Celsius over ten minutes and reached 0 degrees at minute 15.' The first clause uses the change from minute 0 to minute 5 but names the ten-minute interval. Over the recorded first ten minutes, the decrease is 35 - 30 = 5 degrees Celsius. The second clause incorrectly converts missing data into a measured zero.

Write a corrected report: 'The recorded temperature fell from 35 to 30 degrees Celsius between minutes 0 and 10, a decrease of 5 degrees. No reading is available for minute 15.' This reports what the table supports without inventing a later trend. If the original observation itself is in doubt, retain its value and annotate the concern rather than silently editing it to fit the paragraph.

Use a four-part check for each numerical statement: quantity, value, unit and reference interval or group. A true number attached to the wrong interval is still a misleading statement. Keep a record of the correction so another reader can see that the summary changed while the original observations were preserved. This is a consistency check, not proof that the fictional measurements accurately represent a real object.
practice: What decrease is recorded from minute 0 to minute 5, and from minute 0 to minute 10?
Rewrite 'The temperature remained at 30 degrees Celsius through minute 15' to match the available record.
If a summary and raw record disagree, why should the raw record not simply be changed to match the summary?
answers: A decrease of 2 degrees Celsius over the first five minutes, and 5 degrees Celsius over the first ten.
One version: 'The recorded temperature was 30 degrees Celsius at minute 10; minute 15 was not recorded.' The later temperature is unknown from this table.
That would hide the discrepancy and invent evidence. Preserve the raw entry, investigate the mismatch, and document any justified correction or revision separately.
lessons.adaptation: Read the row labels aloud and use separate cards for values and missing entries. Learners can dictate a correction while pointing to the supporting rows.

lessons.title: Distinguish plotted observations from estimates and forecasts
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Label observed values, interpolation and extrapolation, and explain why a connecting line does not supply additional measurements.
lessons.materials: Paper axes or the verbal data description below; all plant-height records are fictional.
lesson: A supplied seedling record gives height at day 0 as 4 cm, day 2 as 6 cm, day 4 as 8 cm and day 6 as 10 cm. Plot those four observations as distinct points. A learner draws straight segments through them and extends the line. The points represent listed records; the line represents an assumed relation between day and height. There is no listed measurement for every position on the line.

The assumed rule is height = 4 + day, in centimetres, or an increase of 1 cm per day. At day 3 it gives 7 cm. This estimate lies inside the observed time range and is interpolation. At day 8 it gives 12 cm, outside the observed time range, so it is extrapolation. Neither value becomes an observation merely because it can be read from the drawn line.

A later fictional observation reports 10.5 cm at day 8. Keep it as a new observed point and compare it with the previous 12 cm prediction; do not move the point to make the line look correct. The discrepancy is 1.5 cm. It may motivate examining the model, observations and growing conditions. Four earlier points following a simple pattern did not establish that the same rate must continue indefinitely.

Use a key distinguishing recorded points from assumed or extended lines, and label any estimate in the accompanying text. Interpolation still depends on a model; hidden changes can occur between measurements. Extrapolation adds the question of whether the model remains applicable beyond the observed range. A report should preserve that distinction even when the arithmetic is exact.
practice: Using the original straight-line rule, estimate height at day 5. Is this interpolation, extrapolation or an observation in the supplied table?
Using that same original rule, estimate height at day 10 and identify the type of estimate.
How should a report handle the later day-8 observation of 10.5 cm when the previous model predicted 12 cm?
answers: 9 cm. It is interpolation within days 0 through 6; day 5 was not a listed observation.
14 cm. It is extrapolation beyond the original observed time range.
Record the observation separately, retain the earlier prediction as a prediction, and report their 1.5 cm discrepancy. Review the model or data rather than changing the observation to fit the line.
lessons.adaptation: Provide a table instead of requiring a visual plot, and mark entries as observed or estimated in words. Learners may explain the distinction orally before calculating.

lessons.title: Keep quantifiers and conditions when summarizing a claim
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Preserve the scope of words such as some, all and under these conditions, and identify a summary that becomes stronger than its evidence.
lessons.materials: Paper claim cards and three fictional filter-model records, read aloud if needed.
lesson: Small words can determine the strength of a scientific statement. Some states that at least part of a group has a property, without claiming every member does. All covers every member of the named group. In these trials restricts a statement to particular records. May signals a possibility in the intended context, not a guaranteed result. A summary can become inaccurate by dropping just one of these qualifiers.

Use an original paper light-token model with ten incoming tokens per filter card. The records show A transmits six, B transmits four and C transmits zero. 'Some of these three filter cards transmitted tokens' is supported. 'Every filter card transmitted tokens' is contradicted by C. 'All possible filter materials block some light in every setting' goes beyond the three supplied records and the model's scope.

Quantifiers must stay attached to their reference group. 'All three cards in this model transmitted fewer than ten tokens' fits the record, but replacing it with 'all filters everywhere transmit fewer than ten' removes the restriction. Likewise, zero transmitted tokens in C's record is an observation within this model; it does not by itself establish behavior at every wavelength, angle or condition of a real material.

Revise precisely rather than making every statement vague. If the record supports an exact count, use it: 'Two of the three modeled cards transmitted at least one token, with counts of six, four and zero across A, B and C.' State the evidence boundary and keep important conditions. A cautious-sounding word is not a substitute for checking whether the underlying claim is actually supported.
practice: Is 'All three modeled cards transmitted fewer than ten tokens' supported? Check each count.
Revise 'All filters allow some light through' to match only the supplied model records.
Why does adding 'possibly' to a claim about every real filter not repair the absence of evidence about those materials and conditions?
answers: Yes. Six, four and zero are each less than ten, and the claim is restricted to the three modeled cards.

One acceptable revision is 'Two of the three modeled filter cards transmitted tokens: A transmitted six and B four; C transmitted zero.' Equivalent summaries must preserve the limited group and C's zero.
The word weakens the certainty but does not provide the missing evidence or define the scope. The summary should report the actual records and identify what remains unknown.
lessons.adaptation: Underline the group name and circle the quantifier in each sentence. Learners can sort claim cards into supported, contradicted and not established, explaining their choices aloud.

lessons.title: Describe a scientific figure so its information is available in text
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Write a useful figure introduction and fuller text description preserving labels, values and the stated context without inventing an explanation.
lessons.materials: Paper for the original chart described here, or its values as a table; color is not needed.
lesson: A chart can carry essential information that a reader needs in another form. For a complex figure, a brief identifying description can point to a fuller explanation containing the important labels, relationships and values. The right detail depends on the figure's purpose and surrounding text. A decorative description of colors alone may omit the information needed to understand the evidence.

Use this original fictional chart: three vertical bars show counted seedlings on day 7 in trays A, B and C. The vertical axis is number of counted seedlings, starting at zero with ticks at 3, 6 and 9. A has 6, B has 9 and C has 3. A short description could say, 'Bar chart of day-7 seedling counts in three fictional trays; values are given in the following text.' A fuller description then names the three counts and explains that B is highest and C lowest.

Keep observed information separate from an inferred explanation. The chart gives no initial seed counts, tray areas or treatment assignments. Therefore it does not show that B had the highest germination percentage or that a treatment caused its higher count. A clear description preserves those limits instead of adding a persuasive story. If exact values matter to the reader's task, include them in text or an accessible table rather than only saying that the bars differ.

Review the description without looking at the drawing. Can the reader identify the quantity, units or count type, time, groups and relevant comparisons? Avoid phrases such as 'the green one' when a group label is available. This paper exercise practices communicating essential figure content; producing a fully accessible digital document also depends on structure, implementation and user needs beyond this one description.
practice: Write a fuller text description that includes the chart's quantity, day, tray labels and all three values.
How many more seedlings were counted in B than A? Can the chart alone establish that B had the higher germination percentage?
Why is 'Three colored bars, one tall and two shorter' insufficient for a reader who needs the scientific information?
answers: One version: 'The fictional chart records seedling counts on day 7: tray A has 6, B has 9 and C has 3. B has the largest count and C the smallest. The vertical count axis starts at zero.' Equivalent descriptions should retain all labels, values and context.
Three more were counted in B. No germination percentage can be established without a suitable initial seed denominator and a clear definition of what was counted.
It omits the measured quantity, group identities, values and day. Relative visual appearance alone cannot answer the same questions as the chart.
lessons.adaptation: Use a partner who receives only the text and asks questions about missing information. Spoken descriptions and a labeled data list can be used without drawing or seeing the chart.

lessons.title: Revise a scientific explanation after targeted feedback
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Use feedback to repair a specific reasoning error while keeping the observations, mechanism and limitations distinct.
lessons.materials: Paper copies of the original cooling record, draft and feedback; use only the supplied fictional data.
lesson: Read this fictional record: equal amounts of the same liquid in matching containers start at 50 degrees Celsius in a 20-degree room. One container has a sleeve and one is bare. At minute 10 the sleeved record is 36 degrees and the bare record is 30. These are supplied paper values. The draft explanation says, 'The sleeve made heat because its container was hotter. It stopped all cooling.'

Give feedback tied to a specific sentence and record: 'Compare both final readings with their 50-degree starting value. Did either container get warmer during the recorded interval?' The sleeved reading fell by 14 degrees and the bare reading by 20. Being warmer than the other container at the end does not mean warming occurred over time. The draft confuses a comparison between containers with a change within one container.

A revision could say, 'Both recorded temperatures fell. The sleeved container had the smaller decrease over ten minutes. Under the stated matching conditions, that pattern is consistent with a sleeve reducing the rate of net energy transfer to cooler surroundings; these two readings alone do not establish every transfer pathway or performance in other settings.' The revision uses the record, proposes a bounded explanation and removes the unsupported claim that cooling stopped.

Check whether the revision answers the feedback without inventing evidence. Replacing made heat with kept all heat would still conflict with the decrease and overstate the account. More tests and a clearer measurement record could strengthen the explanation; simply adding 'scientifically proven' could not. Keep both the original draft and revision when reviewing learning so the changed reasoning is visible. No real heating activity or insulation selection is required.
practice: Calculate each recorded temperature decrease over ten minutes.
Explain the difference between 'the sleeved container was warmer than the bare one at minute 10' and 'the sleeved container warmed up.'
Revise 'The sleeve stopped all cooling' in one or two sentences using the supplied evidence and an appropriate limit.
answers: Sleeved: 50 - 36 = 14 degrees Celsius. Bare: 50 - 30 = 20 degrees Celsius.
The first compares two containers at the same time. The second asserts a temperature increase within one container over time, which these records contradict.

Accept a revision stating that the sleeved record still cooled but had a smaller decrease in this comparison. It should avoid a universal effectiveness claim and distinguish the supplied pattern from complete proof of a mechanism.
lessons.adaptation: Read the draft and feedback aloud, then let the learner dictate a revision. Assess the change in reasoning separately from spelling or fluent independent reading.

lessons.title: Build a scientific reading brief from records, a model and a caption
lessons.audience: Supported readers with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Combine an original passage and data record into a short explanation that labels evidence, calculations, model assumptions and remaining questions.
lessons.materials: Paper for a one-page brief and the complete fictional study record below; no experiment, heating or equipment is required.
lesson: Read this original study description: 'Three paper trials compare bare and sleeved matching containers. Each uses equal amounts of the same liquid, a recorded start of 50 degrees Celsius and a room at 20 degrees. At minute 10, bare-container readings are 30, 31 and 29 degrees; sleeved readings are 36, 35 and 37. No measurements after minute 10 are supplied. The description does not record how positions or condition order were assigned.' Treat this as a fictional reading dossier, not a report of an experiment performed by FieldForge.

Extract observations before writing a conclusion. The bare-group final mean is (30 + 31 + 29)/3 = 30 degrees, and the sleeved mean is (36 + 35 + 37)/3 = 36. All six readings are below the common 50-degree start. The group means therefore correspond to average decreases of 20 and 14 degrees over the stated interval. The six-degree difference is a difference between final means, not evidence that either group warmed up.

Use a thermal-transfer model to propose a limited explanation: a sleeve can alter transfers between the container and cooler surroundings. Under the matching assumptions, the supplied pattern is consistent with slower net energy loss in the sleeved condition. Check alternatives and evidence gaps, including measurement quality, position effects and the unrecorded assignment method. Three fictional trials do not establish performance for every material, duration or setup, and no later temperature should be invented from these records.

Prepare a brief with a descriptive title, a small labeled value table or text description, one calculation with units, a claim linked to the records, a possible mechanism with assumptions, and one specific next evidence need. Attribute the numbers to this lesson's fictional dossier. For a figure caption, identify the ten-minute endpoint and the groups, and provide all six values in accompanying text. Keep an observed pattern, a calculated summary and a model-based explanation distinguishable to the reader.
practice: Calculate the two final group means and their difference. State why neither mean demonstrates warming from the start.
Write a three- or four-sentence explanation containing a numerical comparison, a possible mechanism and a limitation grounded in the dossier.
Name one specific additional record that would help assess the explanation, and give a suitable caption or text introduction for the six final readings.
answers: Bare mean 30 degrees Celsius; sleeved mean 36; difference 6 degrees. Both are below the 50-degree start, so both groups cooled on average, and all individual listed readings also fell.

Accept an explanation reporting the smaller average decrease for the sleeved group, connecting it cautiously to altered energy transfer under the matching assumptions, and naming a real gap such as assignment, position effects, measurement quality or later-time behavior. Reject claims of proven universal performance or heat creation.

Possible records include measurement method and uncertainty, condition/position assignments, or readings at additional stated times. A caption could be 'Fictional ten-minute container temperatures in degrees Celsius: bare 30, 31, 29; sleeved 36, 35, 37; all started at 50.' Equivalent descriptions must identify groups, units, endpoint and values.
lessons.adaptation: Allow a spoken brief with a partner recording it. Record which calculations, readings and explanations were independent, prompted or modeled; this exercise is a learning record rather than a certification.

lessons.title: Plan mixed review from observed work
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Choose a small set of previously taught skills, record the help used, and use actual work to select the next review task.
lessons.materials: Paper review cards, a learning record and a cover for the answer guidance; no timer or score scale is needed.
lesson: A review session can ask a learner to choose a method instead of repeating one announced operation. Choose three skills already taught, such as reading a notice, finding an elapsed time and making equal groups. Before mixing them, check that the words and representations are accessible. If a skill is unfamiliar, teach it with a worked example first. A difficult first encounter is different from forgetting something previously practiced.

Try this original pair of cards: A says 'Four packets each contain 6 counters; find the total.' B says 'A session starts at 09:15 and ends at 09:50; find its duration.' A needs equal-group reasoning: 4 x 6 = 24 counters. B needs elapsed-time reasoning: 35 minutes. Naming the quantity and its unit helps select the method. Merely seeing two numbers does not mean the same operation suits both cards.

Record the card, the first attempt, the learner's explanation and the support given. For example: 'A: 24, independently explained as four sixes. B: 35 after a facilitator drew the clock intervals.' Keep both outcomes; the second is evidence of success with that support, not evidence that the duration was found independently. A learner's confidence is useful to discuss but cannot substitute for the recorded work. Do not combine these observations into a diagnostic label.

Check an attempt against the answer, discuss a specific mismatch, then use a new example. For B, a later card could run from 10:20 to 10:55. Schedule another short revisit after a gap and note whether the method is selected without the same prompt. Adjust the gap and difficulty to the observed work rather than promising one fixed schedule suits everyone. Retain the original attempt alongside the retry so that a corrected copy is not mistaken for a fresh solution.
practice: A learner writes 42 for six packets of 7 and explains six equal groups without a hint. What should the support record say?
A learner finds 25 minutes from 14:10 to 14:35 only after seeing a fully worked solution. Write an accurate record and propose a fresh retry.
A learner confidently gives 09:45 minus 09:20 as 65 minutes. What evidence and next action should guide the review?
answers: Record 42 counters and the equal-group explanation as independent on that attempt. One successful item does not establish every multiplication skill.
Record 25 minutes as completed after a model, preserving the first attempt if any. A suitable new card is 15:05 to 15:30, also 25 minutes, attempted before revealing its solution.

Use the incorrect duration and explanation as the evidence, not the confidence alone. Show that 09:20 to 09:45 spans 25 minutes, discuss the error, then try a different interval and record the support used.
lessons.adaptation: Allow spoken explanations, large print or movable cards. Separate help with reading the card from help choosing or carrying out the mathematical method.

lessons.title: Read a changed timetable and support an inference
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Combine a supported narrative with time calculations while distinguishing directly stated facts from a reasonable inference.
lessons.materials: The original passage below, paper and an optional clock face; preview revised, reserve and postponed aloud.
lesson: A revised notice has been changed; to reserve here means to keep something available; postponed means moved to a later time. Read this original passage with support as needed: 'Mina and Cal arrived at the reading room at 09:35. Their copied notice said it would open at 09:30. A new sign on the door read: Revised opening today: 10:00. At 09:45 a volunteer came outside. She said, I can reserve your two seats. Mina put away the clock sheet she had planned to use inside. Cal said, We still have time to read the short story on the bench. They opened the story together.'

List direct facts before drawing conclusions. They arrived at 09:35; the revised opening is 10:00; the volunteer spoke at 09:45. The text does not state why the opening changed or promise when the activity inside will finish. From arrival to the revised opening is 25 minutes. From the volunteer's appearance to that opening is 15 minutes. Both durations are correct because they start at different events.

An inference combines details with reasoning. It is reasonable to infer that Mina's planned indoor clock activity is being delayed: the room is not open yet and she puts away its sheet. The passage does not directly say she feels angry, and the same actions would fit other feelings. Write 'This suggests...' for a supported interpretation and cite the relevant actions. Do not add an imagined emotion or cause as though it were printed in the passage.

Check which notice applies. The copied notice gives the older 09:30 time; the door explicitly labels today's 10:00 opening as revised. In this fictional account that is the update. A seat reservation says something about availability of seats, not that the room has already opened. Retell the sequence using the stated times, then mark an unanswered question separately. Comprehension and time arithmetic can be reviewed together while their errors are recorded separately.
practice: How long after the copied opening time did Mina and Cal arrive, and how long must they wait from arrival until the revised opening?
Which details support the inference that the indoor clock activity was postponed? Does the text establish Mina's exact feeling?
After the volunteer appears, they spend 8 minutes reading. What time is it then, and how many minutes remain until the revised opening?
answers: They arrive 5 minutes after 09:30. From 09:35 to 10:00 they have a 25-minute wait.
The revised opening is later than their arrival, and Mina puts away the sheet intended for use inside. These details support delay; they do not establish her exact feeling.
09:45 plus 8 minutes is 09:53. Seven minutes remain until 10:00.
lessons.adaptation: Read the full passage aloud or share the reading. Record whether help concerned decoding, locating a fact, forming an inference or calculating time; the passage is not a phonics-controlled independent reading test.

lessons.title: Write a clear request from an incomplete record
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Turn a fictional planning record into a concise request that preserves unknown fields and makes the needed reply explicit.
lessons.materials: Paper or a disposable draft document; use only the fictional records supplied here and do not send the request.
lesson: A useful request helps its reader decide what to do next. This original planning record says: 'Group: Cedar reading circle. Requested room: Room B. Day: Thursday 15 October 2026. Time: 14:00 to 14:45. People: 8. Need: confirm the room and eight chairs. Desired reply: by 12:00 Tuesday 13 October 2026. Coordinator contact: not recorded.' The intended reader is the fictional room coordinator. The record describes a request, not an approved booking.

Draft from the supplied facts: 'Please confirm whether Room B and eight chairs are available for Cedar reading circle, eight people, on Thursday 15 October from 14:00 to 14:45. Please reply by 12:00 Tuesday 13 October. If the room is unavailable, please tell us so that we can revise the plan.' Add a private draft note: 'Coordinator contact not recorded; find the agreed contact before sending.' Do not invent an address or imply the request has been delivered.

Review the draft as its reader. It identifies the group, resource, date, interval, number of people, requested decision and reply deadline. The session lasts 45 minutes. The deadline is earlier than the session, allowing time for revision, but that does not guarantee a response. A statement such as 'The room is confirmed' would change the evidence and is unsupported. A reply asking for more information should also remain distinct from an acceptance.

Now consider a revision note: 'Expected people changed to 10; time unchanged; room capacity not checked.' Update both the people count and chair request to 10, and ask whether Room B can accommodate the revised group. Retain the uncertainty about capacity and contact. A complete revision follows the consequences of the changed field; replacing only one occurrence of eight would leave a contradiction. Record what was checked and what still needs a real answer.
practice: Draft the first request in two or three sentences using the original eight-person record. Include the requested reply and its deadline.
Apply the ten-person revision. Name two linked fields that must change and one fact that remains unconfirmed.
A draft says 'Your approved room will be ready at 14:00; we have emailed the coordinator.' Identify the claims unsupported by the supplied record and replace them.
answers: Accept a concise request naming Cedar reading circle, Room B, eight people/eight chairs, 15 October 2026 from 14:00 to 14:45, and asking for availability confirmation by noon on 13 October 2026. The contact must remain unresolved in the draft record.
Change people from 8 to 10 and chairs from 8 to 10. Room capacity/availability and the coordinator contact are still unconfirmed; the request should ask about the revised group.

Approval and delivery of an email are unsupported. A suitable replacement is 'We request Room B for 14:00 to 14:45; availability is awaiting confirmation, and the coordinator contact has not yet been recorded.'
lessons.adaptation: Permit dictation and use a field checklist. Evaluate the clarity and fidelity of the request separately from spelling or typing support.

lessons.title: Choose operations and interpret the remainder
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Solve a mixed whole-number problem and explain why complete kits and storage containers require different treatments of a remainder.
lessons.materials: Paper counters or a drawn inventory; all counts describe fictional classroom cards.
lesson: The original record says a store has 7 unopened packets of 12 cards and 9 loose cards. Seventeen cards are set aside for another task. Each complete practice kit needs 5 cards. First name what is being counted at each step: packets become cards, a reserved number is removed, then available cards become complete kits. Keeping these quantities visible prevents adding seven packets directly to nine cards.

Calculate the inventory: 7 x 12 = 84 packaged cards; 84 + 9 = 93 total; 93 - 17 = 76 available. Then 76 divided by 5 is 15 remainder 1. The answer is 15 complete kits and 1 unassigned card. Check by reversing the division: 15 x 5 + 1 = 76. Sixteen complete kits would require 80 cards, which exceeds the available amount by 4.

Change the question while retaining 76 cards: how many containers are needed if each holds at most 5 cards and every card must be stored? Fifteen full containers hold 75, leaving one card that needs another container. Here the answer is 16 containers, including one partly filled container. Rounding down for complete kits and rounding up for sufficient containers come from the meanings of the questions, not an arbitrary rule that every remainder is treated the same way.

Estimate and inspect the result. About 80 available cards would make about 16 groups of five, so 15 complete kits is plausible; this does not replace the exact inventory. To find an error, keep the intermediate counts and units instead of erasing all work. A correct final number produced from a contradictory inventory is not yet a clear explanation. After feedback, use a new inventory so the learner must select the steps again.
practice: A new record has 6 packets of 14 cards plus 8 loose cards, with 19 reserved. How many remain available, and how many complete 4-card kits can be made?
For those same available cards, how many containers holding at most 4 each are needed to store every card? Explain the difference from the kit answer.
A learner claims 19 complete 4-card kits can be made from the new inventory. Use multiplication to check the claim and calculate any shortage.
answers: 6 x 14 + 8 - 19 = 73 cards. There are 18 complete kits and 1 card left, since 18 x 4 + 1 = 73.
19 containers: 18 full containers hold 72 and the last holds 1. A partly filled container still counts, whereas a partly filled kit is not a complete kit.
19 x 4 = 76 cards would be required; only 73 are available, a shortage of 3. The claim is not supported.
lessons.adaptation: Represent packets and cards separately with drawings, then connect each drawing to its equation. Record assistance with operation choice separately from assistance with calculation.

lessons.title: Connect fraction, decimal and percent to the same whole
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Translate a part-whole count between representations and compare quantities only after identifying each whole.
lessons.materials: Paper grids or counters for the fictional counts; a calculator may be used after the fraction and denominator are explained.
lesson: In this original review record, 24 of 60 reading cards have been checked. The fraction checked is 24/60, which simplifies to 2/5 by dividing numerator and denominator by 12. Dividing 24 by 60 gives 0.4, or 40%. These are three representations of the same share of the same 60-card collection. The unchecked share is 36/60 = 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%; the two shares total one whole.

Later, 42 of those same 60 cards have been checked. The new share is 42/60 = 7/10 = 0.7 = 70%. Eighteen additional cards have been checked. The percentage rises by 30 percentage points because 70 - 40 = 30. If asked for the relative increase in the checked count, use the earlier 24 as the reference: 18/24 = 75%. These questions have different denominators and therefore different numerical answers.

Now compare different collections. One quarter of 48 cards is 12 cards; one half of 20 cards is 10 cards. Although one half is the larger fraction, it describes fewer cards here because its whole is smaller. Label every fraction or percent with its reference set. A bare statement such as 'half is more' is incomplete when it means a number of objects from differently sized collections.

To check a translation, reconstruct the part: 0.4 x 60 = 24. To check a comparison, show both counts and both denominators. If a record supplies only '40% checked' without the collection size, the number of checked cards is unknown. A diagram can show the fraction of a generic whole, but it cannot supply a missing total. Write the missing information as a question rather than selecting a convenient number.
practice: Thirty of 80 labels have been reviewed. Give the share as a simplest fraction, decimal and percent, and state the unreviewed count.
A fixed 80-label collection goes from 30 reviewed to 50 reviewed. Find the added count and the increase in percentage points.
Compare one third of 45 tokens with two fifths of 30 tokens. Which fraction is larger, and which actual token count is larger?
answers: 30/80 = 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%; 50 labels remain unreviewed.
20 more labels. The shares are 37.5% and 62.5%, so the increase is 25 percentage points.
Two fifths (0.4) exceeds one third (about 0.333), but one third of 45 is 15 tokens and two fifths of 30 is 12. The first collection contributes the larger count because the wholes differ.
lessons.adaptation: Draw equal partitions of a labeled whole or speak the part and total before using symbols. Record whether a hint supplied the denominator or merely helped with division.

lessons.title: Choose perimeter, area or volume before calculating
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Match a question to length, area or volume, calculate from consistent dimensions, and state the corresponding units.
lessons.materials: Paper sketches of an ideal rectangle and rectangular prism; no construction, cutting or actual capacity measurement is required.
lesson: A fictional flat rectangle has side lengths 12 cm and 8 cm. A question about the length of its boundary asks for perimeter: 12 + 8 + 12 + 8 = 40 cm. A question about the region covered by its face asks for area: 12 x 8 = 96 square centimetres, written cm^2. The dimensions are the same, but the requested quantities differ. Drawing a boundary and shading a face can make that distinction visible before choosing a formula.

Imagine an ideal rectangular prism with that 12 cm by 8 cm base and a perpendicular height of 3 cm. Its geometric volume is 12 x 8 x 3 = 288 cubic centimetres, written cm^3. Conceptually it has three 1-cm-thick layers, each containing 96 unit cubes. This differs from the base's area and from the area of all its faces. The exercise gives ideal dimensions, not wall thickness or a usable filling level for a real container.

Unit conversion must follow the quantity. Since 1 m is 100 cm, one square metre contains 10,000 square centimetres, and one cubic metre contains 1,000,000 cubic centimetres. Thus the rectangle's 96 cm^2 is 0.0096 m^2, while the prism's 288 cm^3 is 0.000288 m^3. Dividing either by 100 merely because the length conversion uses 100 would give the wrong quantity conversion.

Use a decision sentence before calculation: 'I need boundary length, so I will add the four sides'; 'I need face area, so I will multiply two perpendicular lengths'; or 'I need prism volume, so I will multiply base area by perpendicular height.'
