Inspect the result's units and check the dimensions use the same length unit. A neatly computed number with the wrong unit still answers the wrong question. If the shape or required dimensions are missing, state that limitation.
practice: A new rectangle is 15 cm by 6 cm. Find its perimeter and area, labeling each quantity and unit.
A rectangular prism has that 15 cm by 6 cm base and height 4 cm. Find its volume. Does the base area alone answer the volume question?
A learner writes that 90 cm^2 equals 0.9 m^2 by dividing by 100. Correct the conversion and explain the needed factor.
answers: Perimeter 2 x (15 + 6) = 42 cm; area 15 x 6 = 90 cm^2.
Volume 15 x 6 x 4 = 360 cm^3. The base area is only 90 cm^2; a height is also needed to determine this prism's volume.
90/10,000 = 0.009 m^2. A square metre has 100 by 100 centimetre squares, so the area factor is 10,000, not 100.
lessons.adaptation: Use tactile or drawn edges, faces and layers, or describe them orally. Record whether support was needed to choose the quantity, use a formula, calculate or convert units.

lessons.title: Read a schedule across midnight and compare rates
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Calculate an interval across midnight and distinguish a rate over active time from a rate over a whole session.
lessons.materials: A paper 24-hour clock or timeline; all times use the same fictional clock with no time-zone or clock-setting change.
lesson: A fictional sorting session starts at 23:20 on Day 1 and ends at 00:20 on Day 2. Split the interval at midnight: 40 minutes from 23:20 to 24:00, then 20 minutes to 00:20. The total is 60 minutes. The day labels matter; subtracting 23:20 from 00:20 as if both belonged to the same date obscures the intended interval. Here 24:00 marks the end of Day 1, the same instant as 00:00 at the start of Day 2.

The record includes a 12-minute pause and says all other session time was active sorting. Active time is 60 - 12 = 48 minutes. A total of 144 cards was sorted, all during active time. The active-time average rate is 144/48 = 3 cards per minute. Across the entire elapsed session the average is 144/60 = 2.4 cards per minute. Both calculations are valid because their denominators answer different questions.

Write a complete rate statement: 'The session averaged 3 cards per active minute, excluding the recorded pause.' Do not quietly use that number as the whole-session average. Neither average says exactly three cards were completed in every individual minute. The record could contain faster and slower intervals. A whole-session rate includes the pause in its denominator even though no cards were sorted during that pause.

Before comparing two sessions, align their definitions. Compare active-time rates with active-time rates, or elapsed-session rates with elapsed-session rates. Check counts, durations and the treatment of breaks. If the pause duration is missing, an active-time rate cannot be reconstructed from the total elapsed time alone. For actual clocks, dates and changes in clock settings can require additional information; the fixed-clock assumption deliberately removes those complications here.
practice: A fresh session runs from 23:35 on Day 1 to 00:25 on Day 2 on the same unchanged clock. It has one 10-minute pause and no other inactive time. Find elapsed and active minutes.
That session sorts 120 cards during active time. Find its active-time and whole-session average rates, then compare each with the worked session using the same denominator type.
A third record reports 90 cards in a 45-minute session but leaves the pause duration blank. Which average rate can be calculated, and which remains unresolved?
answers: 25 minutes to midnight plus 25 afterward gives 50 elapsed minutes; subtract 10 for 40 active minutes.
120/40 = 3 cards per active minute; 120/50 = 2.4 cards per elapsed-session minute. Each matches the corresponding worked-session average, although totals and durations differ.
The whole-session average is 90/45 = 2 cards per minute. The active-time average is unresolved because active duration is unknown; a blank pause field must not be treated as a zero-minute pause.
lessons.adaptation: Mark midnight on a line and move along each interval. Allow a calculator for division while asking the learner to name and justify each denominator.

lessons.title: Inspect a distribution before choosing an average
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Compute and interpret mean and median for a small complete list, then explain how an unrecorded value limits the conclusion.
lessons.materials: Paper number cards for the original fictional durations; no real learner speed comparison or performance ranking is required.
lesson: Five recorded durations for a fictional paper task are 2, 3, 3, 4 and 13 minutes. The sum is 25 minutes, so the mean is 25/5 = 5 minutes. The sorted middle value is 3, so the median is 3 minutes. Keep the ordered list beside both summaries. It shows why they differ: the 13-minute duration affects the total strongly, while the third position remains 3.

Choose a summary for the question, and describe its limits. The mean connects the five-record total to the count: 5 records times 5 minutes equals 25 minutes. The median locates the middle ordered record and is less affected by the size of this one high value. Neither summary is a time achieved by every record, and neither alone describes the full spread. Report the observed range as well when useful: minimum 2, maximum 13, difference 11 minutes.

A sixth row says 'duration not recorded.' It is not an observed zero. The known-record mean remains 5 and the known-record median remains 3, but a six-record mean cannot be found without the missing value. Keep the sixth row visible and label which five records were used. Removing the row without mentioning it would hide an evidence gap; entering zero would invent a measurement.

Test the sensitivity by supplying alternative fictional sixth values. If it were 1, the six-record total would be 26, mean 26/6 = 4 1/3, and median 3. If it were 20, the total would be 45, mean 7.5, and median (3 + 4)/2 = 3.5. These are conditional calculations, not recovered data. Do not select the version that gives the preferred result and treat it as the missing observation.
practice: For the fresh complete list 3, 4, 4, 5, 14 minutes, calculate sum, mean, median and range.
An additional duration is unrecorded. A learner inserts zero and reports a six-record mean of 5 minutes. What is wrong, and what can be reported from the known records?
Suppose a later verified record supplies the missing duration as 6 minutes. Recalculate the six-record mean and median; keep this separate from the previous unknown case.
answers: Sum 30 minutes; mean 30/5 = 6 minutes; median 4 minutes; range 14 - 3 = 11 minutes.
Zero was invented. For the five known records the mean is 6 and the median is 4; the six-record mean remains unknown until the missing duration is supplied.
The sorted list is 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 14. Sum 36, mean 36/6 = 6 minutes, median (4 + 5)/2 = 4.5 minutes. The mean happens to stay the same while the median changes.
lessons.adaptation: Arrange movable cards and point to middle positions. Record help with sorting, choosing a denominator and calculating separately; do not interpret task durations as a measure of a learner's worth or ability.

lessons.title: Check a scientific comparison with unequal sample sizes
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Compare observed proportions with their denominators and separate a descriptive result from a causal explanation.
lessons.materials: The fictional seed-count dossier below and paper; this is a data exercise, not a request to grow or handle seeds.
lesson: An original fictional dossier reports two seed groups observed at a stated endpoint. Group A has 8 germinated seeds out of 10 recorded seeds. Group B has 14 germinated out of 20 recorded seeds. A germinated seed is defined here as one with a visible root by day 5. The dossier does not record how seeds were assigned or whether growing conditions matched. First preserve the definition, endpoint, numerator and denominator for each group.

Group B has more germinated seeds by count: 14 compared with 8. Group A has the greater observed germination proportion: 8/10 = 80%, compared with 14/20 = 70%. The difference is 10 percentage points. These statements can both be true. Comparing counts answers how many; comparing proportions answers what share of each recorded group. For the combined recorded seeds, use (8 + 14)/(10 + 20) = 22/30, about 73.3%, rather than the unweighted mean of 80% and 70%.

A descriptive claim is 'At day 5, the recorded proportion was higher in A.' A causal claim such as 'A's treatment caused better germination' needs information these records do not provide. Different initial seed characteristics, assignments or conditions could affect the comparison. The counts also do not establish the final outcome at a later day. A correct percentage calculation does not repair an incomplete study design or make the observed difference certain to recur.

For a paper plan of a more informative comparison, specify the question, seed population, group assignment method, intended differing condition, other conditions to keep comparable, endpoint and scoring definition. Record initial group counts and every outcome, including missing or uncertain observations. Random assignment and repeated trials can strengthen a design but do not guarantee identical groups or eliminate every uncertainty. This review asks for an evidence plan, not an actual experiment or a statistical significance claim.
practice: A fresh fictional record gives C: 9 germinated of 12 seeds; D: 16 of 24. Compare counts and proportions, giving the percentage-point difference to one decimal place.
Calculate the combined observed germination proportion for C and D. Why is a simple average of the two group percentages inappropriate for this combined seed count?
The fresh record does not describe assignments or conditions. Rewrite 'C's treatment definitely caused more germination' as a supported statement and name one specific missing record.
answers: D has more germinated seeds by count (16 versus 9). C has the larger proportion: 75% versus about 66.7%, a difference of about 8.3 percentage points.
(9 + 16)/(12 + 24) = 25/36, about 69.4%. The groups have different numbers of seeds; a simple average would give each group equal weight instead of each recorded seed.

Accept: 'At the recorded endpoint, C's observed proportion was higher, but these counts alone do not establish a treatment cause.' Missing records could include seed assignment, initial seed characteristics, matching conditions or the exact endpoint/scoring definition for this fresh record.
lessons.adaptation: Draw two differently sized groups and label numerator and denominator. Let a learner dictate the claim while another records it, noting support with arithmetic separately from support with evidence reasoning.

lessons.title: Trace an algorithm with missing data and boundary cases
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Follow ordered paper rules exactly, preserve identifiers, and use boundary or invalid-input cases to reveal a rule's limits.
lessons.materials: Paper records with identifier and quantity columns, plus an output column; the rule is supplied in full below.
lesson: An algorithm needs precise instructions and defined inputs. This original inventory exercise accepts a nonblank unique ID and either a nonnegative whole-number quantity or a blank quantity. Before classifying any row, flag missing or duplicated IDs and quantities outside that allowed form for correction; do not classify flagged rows. For each remaining row: if quantity is blank, output NEEDS CHECK; otherwise, if quantity is at least 5, output READY; otherwise output LOW. These are labels defined only for this exercise.

Trace these valid-ID records in order: R1 has quantity 5; R2 has 0; R3 is blank; R4 has 8. R1 is READY because at least 5 includes equality. R2 is LOW because zero is a recorded whole-number quantity below 5. R3 is NEEDS CHECK because blank is missing, not zero. R4 is READY. Write an output beside its original ID so a later sort cannot detach a label from the record it describes.

Now introduce a second row labeled R2 with quantity 7. The ID is no longer unique. Under the stated validation rule, flag both R2 rows and withhold their classification until the records are corrected; choosing the first row silently is not an authorized repair. Preserve both raw rows and the reason for the flag. A duplicated name could describe different items, but this exercise requires unique IDs, so a display title cannot resolve the ambiguity.

Use test cases deliberately. Quantities 4, 5 and 6 test the decision boundary; zero tests a valid low value; blank tests missing data; a negative or fractional quantity tests input validation. Changing 'at least 5' to 'greater than 5' would change the output at 5. An algorithm may execute consistently and still fail its intended purpose if a rule is wrong. Keep a trace of the supplied rule before proposing and checking a revision.
practice: Classify unique-ID rows S1: 4, S2: 5, S3: 6, S4: blank and S5: 0 using the supplied rules.
Two rows share ID T1, one with quantity 3 and one with 9; another unique row T2 has quantity -1. What must happen before classification?
Someone rewrites the decision as 'if quantity > 5, READY; otherwise LOW,' while preserving the original blank and validation checks. Which of 4, 5 and 6 changes label, and why?
answers: S1 LOW; S2 READY; S3 READY; S4 NEEDS CHECK; S5 LOW. Five is included in the READY range, and zero is distinct from blank.

Flag both T1 rows because the ID is duplicated, and flag T2 because -1 is outside the allowed nonnegative whole-number input. Do not classify these flagged rows or silently choose a replacement value.
Only 5 changes, from READY to LOW. The strict > comparison excludes equality; 4 stays LOW and 6 stays READY.
lessons.adaptation: Read one rule at a time and move a marker through a trace table. Distinguish assistance reading an operator from assistance deciding which branch applies; all work can remain on paper.

lessons.title: Repair an incorrect model and test a fresh case
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Identify the assumption behind an incorrect equation, repair it, and distinguish copying a correction from using the method on a new case.
lessons.materials: Paper model cards and a calculator if desired; all times are fictional estimates, not measured production rates.
lesson: A fictional brief says: 'For a run of at least one card, setup takes 6 minutes once per run, and each card takes 2 further minutes. Work happens in sequence with no overlap.' For n cards, total time T in minutes is 6 + 2n. For 15 cards, T = 6 + 30 = 36 minutes. The 6-minute term counts one setup, while 2n counts a repeated per-card amount. Labeling the two terms explains why the rule matches the brief.

An incorrect draft writes T = (6 + 2)n and gives 120 minutes for 15 cards. Its arithmetic is consistent with that equation, but the equation counts the setup once for each card: 15 setups instead of one. The difference is 120 - 36 = 84 minutes, equal to the 14 extra setups times 6 minutes. Correcting the arithmetic alone would miss the modeling error. Revise the rule and the explanation of what each term counts.

Check the repaired rule with more than one input. At n = 1, both equations give 8, so that case cannot distinguish them. At n = 2, the intended model gives 10, while the incorrect one gives 16. The brief covers positive whole-number runs. At n = 0, the expression 6 + 2n gives 6 algebraically, but the brief does not say whether a canceled run triggers setup. An operational answer for zero cards therefore needs a stated cancellation rule.

After discussing the error, hide the correction and offer a fresh brief with different values. Ask the learner to write an equation, label its terms and test a case. Record whether the equation was independent, prompted or copied from a model. Retrying the same visible answer shows a different kind of evidence from applying the structure to a new case. Keep limitations, such as the assumed constant per-card time, with the result instead of presenting the model as a measured guarantee.
practice: A new brief has one 4-minute setup plus 3 minutes per card, for positive whole-number runs with no overlap. Write the rule and find the time for 8 cards.
A draft for that new brief uses (4 + 3)n. Explain its error and select a positive test value that distinguishes it from the correct model.
The correct new expression evaluates to 4 at n = 0. Does the brief establish that canceling an empty run takes 4 minutes? State the missing rule.
answers: T = 4 + 3n minutes. At n = 8, T = 4 + 24 = 28 minutes.
It counts the 4-minute setup once per card. For example n = 2 gives 14 under the wrong rule and 10 under the correct rule; n = 1 would not distinguish them.

No. The brief covers positive runs and does not specify whether setup occurs when no cards are processed. Ask whether an empty/canceled run incurs setup before interpreting the zero-input value operationally.
lessons.adaptation: Use one setup card and repeated per-item cards to represent the terms. Record help identifying the fixed amount separately from help with multiplication or equation notation.

lessons.title: Complete a transfer task and choose the next review
lessons.audience: Learners revisiting taught skills with a facilitator; adults may use age-respectful examples
lessons.goal: Produce a small plan that reconciles materials and time, respond to a changed requirement, and choose further practice from recorded evidence.
lessons.materials: The fictional reading-room brief below, paper and a support record; no booking or actual event is requested.
lesson: This original brief plans for 14 participant seats, arranged in pairs. Each pair needs 4 cards, and 30 usable cards are available. The room interval is 09:40 to 10:25. A proposed sequence has a 5-minute welcome, three 10-minute practice rounds and one 5-minute break, all in sequence with no overlap. For this exercise, transitions require no additional time. Actual attendance and any facilitator seating needs have not been recorded. State these assumptions instead of treating them as observed facts.

First reconcile the materials: 14 participant seats make 7 pairs, requiring 7 x 4 = 28 cards, with 2 cards left from 30. Then reconcile the clock: the room interval is 45 minutes. The sequence takes 5 + 3 x 10 + 5 = 40 minutes, leaving a 5-minute margin. One feasible timeline is welcome 09:40-09:45, round 1 09:45-09:55, break 09:55-10:00, round 2 10:00-10:10 and round 3 10:10-10:20. The unused interval ends at 10:25.

Now apply a revision: 'Plan for 16 participant seats in pairs; card stock and session times are unchanged.' Eight pairs need 32 cards, so the 30-card stock is short by 2. The original two spare cards do not cover a new pair's four-card requirement. The timing still fits under the same assumptions, but the materials do not. A revised brief should request two additional usable cards or identify a separately approved change to the requirement; it must not quietly reduce cards per pair and call the original requirement satisfied.

Prepare a plan with its version, participant count, pair count, card calculation, timeline, assumptions and unresolved items. Distinguish planned capacity from actual attendance. After checking it, make a learning record by skill: interpreting the brief, choosing operations, computing quantities, checking time and explaining the revision. Note the first attempt and any prompts or models for each. Choose a specific fresh review task from an observed difficulty; one completed plan is not a certification of every prerequisite skill.
practice: Create a concise version 1 plan for 14 participant seats, including pairs, cards, remaining stock and a timeline that fits the supplied interval.
Revise the materials section for 16 participant seats. State what is short, what can still fit, and at least one item that the brief leaves unconfirmed.

A learner independently gets 8 pairs and 32 cards after the revision but writes '2 cards left' until prompted to compare 32 with stock 30. Write a support record and choose a fresh review question with its answer.
answers: Seven pairs need 28 cards, leaving 2. The supplied sample timeline fits, using 40 of 45 minutes; equivalent sequences are acceptable if all five activities fit without overlap. Keep actual attendance and facilitator seating unresolved.

Eight pairs need 32 cards, creating a shortage of 2. The 40-minute activity sequence still fits the 45-minute interval under the stated assumptions. Actual attendance, facilitator seating or provision of the two additional cards remains unconfirmed.

Record pair and required-card calculations as independent; record the stock comparison and correction from surplus to shortage as prompted. A suitable fresh question is 'Nine pairs need four cards each; stock is 34. Surplus or shortage?' Answer: 36 required, shortage of 2. Attempt it before revealing the answer and record any help.
lessons.adaptation: Allow an oral plan, a timeline drawing or dictated fields. Assign a smaller part of the brief first when needed, and preserve separate records for reading, arithmetic and planning support.
